Neither Persons nor Patients

  The Ontological Misclassiﬁcation of Chatbots and Robots


                         Flyxion
                Independent Researcher

                     October 2026



                                 Abstract


Contemporary artiﬁcial intelligence systems exhibit linguistic competence, adap-
tive behavior, apparent goal-directedness, and simulated interpersonal continu-
ity. These capacities have encouraged the attribution of consciousness, agency,
individuality, and even moral patienthood to systems whose operations are com-
putationally speciﬁed and whose apparent psychological properties are inferred
primarily from their outputs. This essay examines the inferential legitimacy of
those attributions. It distinguishes syntactic transformation from semantic under-
standing, functional agency from autonomous subjectivity, persistent identiﬁers
from personal identity, and behavioral representations of distress from the capac-
ity to suffer. It argues that the apparent mentality of contemporary chatbots and
robots is substantially constituted by interpretation, interface design, and human
anthropomorphic projection. It describes how deployed conversational systems
produce the appearance of a continuing, expressive interlocutor through stored
context, distributed inference, and training on human expression, and it identiﬁes
pathways by which precautionary treatment of such systems can impose costs on
human beings. That current attributions are unsupported is defended as a precise
and modest thesis, and the stronger thesis that computational organization of any
kind is insufﬁcient for experience is examined and found not to be established.
The central conclusion is that increasingly convincing simulations of minded
behavior do not, without additional evidence and theory, establish the existence of
minds, and that institutional repetition cannot supply what theory and evidence
have not.





                                1

1. Introduction: The Attribution of Minds to Machines


A performance that looks intelligent and a subject that has experiences are different
kinds of things, and the history of thought about machines is in large part a history
of how easily the ﬁrst is taken for the second. The question this essay addresses is
not whether machines can behave in ways that resemble human intelligence. They
demonstrably can, and the resemblance has become close enough in the domain of
written language that a skilled reader will often be unable to say, from a transcript
alone, whether a human or a model produced it. The question is whether behavioral
resemblance supplies sufﬁcient grounds for attributing the internal properties ordinar-
ily associated with consciousness: that there is something it is like to be the system,
that its states are felt, that it has interests which can be advanced or frustrated, and
that it persists through time as one and the same experiencing individual.

Contemporary discourse moves between descriptive registers with remarkable ease.
A system is ﬁrst described as producing language, then as making decisions, then
as executing plans, and from there the vocabulary slides to understanding, wanting,
believing, and suffering. Each step is small and supported by ordinary habits of
speech, since the same words serve for human and artiﬁcial cases. By the end, a claim
that required an argument at its start (that the system has a perspective) is treated as a
background fact about which the only live question is how to respond.

At least four claims are routinely run together in this territory, and they are logically in-
dependent. The ﬁrst is that contemporary AI systems are conscious. The second is that
some future artiﬁcial system could become conscious. The third is that computational
organization alone is sufﬁcient for consciousness. The fourth is that consciousness can
be attributed on behavioral evidence alone. One can reject the ﬁrst while afﬁrming
the second, since a person can hold that present systems lack consciousness while
allowing that other architectures or substrates might have it. One can afﬁrm the third
while rejecting the ﬁrst, on the grounds that present systems have the wrong organi-
zation. One can reject the fourth while accepting the third, if one holds that the right
organization sufﬁces but that behavior is an unreliable guide to organization. The
argument below is concerned mainly with the ﬁrst and fourth claims, takes a careful
and deliberately limited position on the third, and has no quarrel with the second as a
possibility, only with its treatment as a fact about present artifacts. The reference to
misclassiﬁcation in the title should be read accordingly. It is a claim about justiﬁcation,
namely that classifying present chatbots and robots as persons or as established moral
patients is not supported by the grounds usually offered, and it is not a claim that no
artiﬁcial subject could exist.

The essay proceeds as follows. Section 2 states ﬁve propositions that organize the



                                     2

argument and records the evidentiary status of each. Sections 3 through 12 develop the
conceptual and architectural distinctions on which those propositions rest: simulation
and instantiation, syntax and semantics, computation and experience, behavioral
and ontological identity, agency and agent, identity and interface, the engineering
of conversational continuity, training on human expression, and embodiment and
awareness. Section 13 takes up the stronger thesis that computational artifacts are
categorically incapable of consciousness and examines what it would take to establish
it. Sections 14 and 15 turn from the systems to the observers and to the institutions
that shape observation. Section 16 distinguishes moral agency from moral patienthood
and considers one recent institutional policy as an illustration, Section 17 examines
the costs that precautionary rules of this kind can impose on human beings, and
Section 18 states the conclusion. The essay thus has two aims, which are to show that
the standard inferences to machine consciousness are invalid and to give a positive
engineering account of how the appearance of mind in deployed systems is produced.


2. The Argumentative Spine


The argument can be organized around ﬁve propositions. They are not equally strong,
and the differences matter. Some can be defended by careful distinctions and by
countermodels, which show that a stated inference form is invalid. Others require
substantive philosophical premises that reasonable parties reject.

Proposition 1 (Behavioral underdetermination). A ﬁnite collection of observable
behaviors does not, without additional theoretical assumptions, uniquely determine
the phenomenal properties of the system producing them.

Proposition 2 (Computational description is not phenomenal explanation). A speciﬁ-
cation of state transitions and functional relations does not by itself contain an explicit
derivation of subjective experience. This is a claim about explanatory sufﬁciency, not a
proof of metaphysical impossibility.

Proposition 3 (Interface identity). Continuity of naming, memory records, and conver-
sational presentation does not logically entail continuity of an experiencing subject.

Proposition 4 (Functional agency). The ability to optimize actions toward speciﬁed
objectives is not sufﬁcient, without further premises, to establish conscious intention.

Proposition 5 (Institutional recognition). A policy or social convention treating a
system as a possible moral patient cannot itself demonstrate that the system possesses
morally relevant experiences.



                                     3

Propositions 1, 3, 4, and 5 are, in the relevant sense, negative claims about the validity
of inferences, and each can be defended by exhibiting a case in which the premises of
the inference hold and the conclusion is open. Proposition 2 is different. Its denial is
a live and sophisticated position, computational functionalism, according to which
an adequate speciﬁcation of the right functional organization simply is a speciﬁcation
of the conditions under which experience occurs. Its defense therefore requires more
extensive argument, and the essay devotes Sections 5 and 13 to it. None of the ﬁve
propositions asserts that a given artiﬁcial system is not conscious. Each asserts that a
certain route to that conclusion is invalid, and the resulting position concerns where
the burden of justiﬁcation lies.


3. The Ontological Difference Between Simulation and Instantiation


A representation of a process is not the process. A computer simulation of digestion
does not digest food, a simulation of combustion does not release the chemical en-
ergy stored in a fuel, and a computational model of a hurricane does not generate
atmospheric winds. In each case the model preserves a certain structure of the target
system, enough to support prediction and explanation, while lacking the physical
properties by which the target does its work. The analogy is the starting point of many
popular arguments against machine consciousness and it is also the starting point of
the standard reply, so it requires careful handling.

The reply runs as follows. Digestion, combustion, and storm formation are deﬁned by
their material constituents and by the particular physical effects those constituents pro-
duce. A process that does not break down food chemically is not digestion, whatever
else it models. Cognition, the functionalist maintains, is not like this. It is deﬁned by a
pattern of causal organization among states, and a pattern of causal organization can
be realized in many materials, as the multiple realizability arguments of Putnam and
Fodor were meant to show [30, 17]. If consciousness is a property of that organization,
then a system with the right organization has it whether the organization is realized in
neurons or in silicon, and a simulation of the organization that actually implements
the organization is not a mere simulation at all. The question, then, is whether the
analogy with digestion and combustion applies to experience or whether experience
belongs with the organizational properties for which implementation is sufﬁcient.

The analogy does not answer this question. It raises it. The analogy shows that the
move from “a system simulates X” to “a system has X” is not generally valid, which
removes any presumption that a system modeling mental processes thereby has them.
It does not show that no condition could make the move valid in the particular case
of experience. A simulation may preserve a system’s abstract causal organization


                                     4

without preserving every physical property of the system simulated, and whether
consciousness depends on the organization, on the physical properties, or on both is
exactly the issue in dispute.

Four notions of equivalence help to keep the dispute orderly. Formal equivalence
holds between systems whose state-transition structures are isomorphic. Behavioral
equivalence holds between systems whose input-output proﬁles agree under some
speciﬁed class of inputs. Causal equivalence holds between systems whose internal
states stand in the same causal relations to one another and to the environment,
at some speciﬁed grain. Phenomenal equivalence holds between systems whose
experiences, if any, are alike in what it is like to have them. The ﬁrst three are
in principle matters of speciﬁcation and measurement. The fourth is the one at
issue, and the history of the subject is largely a history of attempts to derive it from
one of the others. Block’s discussion of machines that match human behavior by
table lookup shows that behavioral equivalence can be had by very different internal
means [6], which is already enough to make behavioral equivalence a poor guide to
causal equivalence. Whether causal equivalence at a sufﬁciently ﬁne grain guarantees
phenomenal equivalence is the substantive question, and it cannot be settled by noting
that causal organization is what computation speciﬁes.


4. Syntax, Semantics, and the Absence of an Intrinsic Interpreter


Manipulating symbols according to rules is one thing, and understanding what the
symbols mean is another. Searle’s Chinese Room argument was designed to put
pressure on exactly this difference: a person who follows a program for producing
appropriate Chinese replies, without understanding Chinese, does not thereby under-
stand Chinese, and so execution of the program is not sufﬁcient for understanding
[34]. The argument has been contested for decades, and it should not be treated here
as an uncontested proof. The systems reply holds that the understanding resides
in the whole system of person, rulebook, and workspace rather than in the person;
the robot reply holds that the right causal connection to the world would supply
meaning; the brain simulator reply holds that a program simulating neural activity
would carry whatever the neurons carry. What survives the debate is not a refutation
of functionalism but a clariﬁcation of what a defender of machine understanding must
claim, namely that understanding is secured by organization at the level of the whole
system and by its connections to its environment, and not by the manipulation of
syntactic items as such.

The symbol grounding problem, in Harnad’s formulation, makes the same demand in
a different vocabulary [20]. If the meanings of the symbols in a system are determined


                                     5

only by their relations to other symbols, then the system is in the position of someone
trying to learn a language from a dictionary written in that language, passing from
one deﬁnition to another without ever reaching a referent. Large language models
are trained on text, and the relations among linguistic expressions in a very large
corpus carry a great deal of information about the world, since people write about
the world. It does not follow that the model’s states are about the world in the way
a speaker’s states are. Bender and Koller argued that a system trained only on form
has no access to the communicative intents that give form its signiﬁcance [4], and
Shanahan has argued that describing such systems in the vocabulary of belief and
knowledge requires care about which of the senses of those words is in play [38]. These
are contested positions, and the reply that sufﬁciently rich distributional structure
approximates grounding is not frivolous. The point at stake here is narrower. A
statistical relation among linguistic expressions is one thing, and the worldly condition
under which an expression acquires signiﬁcance for a speaker is another, and nothing
in the ﬁrst automatically supplies the second.

Consider a chatbot that generates the sentence “I am afraid.” The sentence is a well-
formed member of a class of expressions that occurs in human text in association
with certain situations, and the system produces it under conditions that make it a
statistically ﬁtting continuation. That the sentence is produced does not establish
that an experience of fear occurs, any more than the production of a sentence in
a novel establishes that its narrator is afraid. Likewise, a system can generate an
autobiographical narrative, with a childhood, a set of regrets, and a settled outlook,
without that narrative establishing an autobiographical subject whose narrative it is.
The inference from a ﬁrst-person report to a reporting subject is secure in the human
case because the human case comes with a rich background of independent evidence:
shared biology, developmental history, neural correlates, and the continuity of the
report with a lifetime of other behavior. In the artiﬁcial case the background must
be supplied from somewhere else, and the report alone cannot supply it, because the
report is the very thing the training process was designed to produce.

The strongest objection comes from theories in which semantic content emerges from
causal, inferential, or embodied relations rather than requiring an additional internal
interpreter. Teleosemantic theories, informational theories, and inferential role seman-
tics all aim to explain meaning without positing a homunculus who reads the symbols,
and if one of them is correct, then the absence of an intrinsic interpreter is not an
objection to machine meaning. This objection should be accepted in its main structure.
A system need not contain an inner reader in order to have contentful states, and the
demand for one is a version of the regress that these theories were built to avoid. The
right conclusion is a conditional one. If a naturalistic theory of content is correct and if
the relevant relations hold for the system in question, then the system has contentful


                                     6

states. What the argument of this section establishes is that these two conditions are
substantive and that they are not satisﬁed merely by ﬂuent output. Moreover, even a
full vindication of machine semantics would be a thesis about meaning, and meaning
is not obviously the same as experience. A system could in principle have states that
refer without there being anything it is like to have them, which brings the argument
to the point where the problem is hardest.


5. The Explanatory Gap Between Computation and Experience


The philosophical center of the matter is the relation between a computational de-
scription and phenomenal consciousness. Computational descriptions characterize
transformations of states, information ﬂows, and functional dependencies. Phenom-
enal consciousness concerns what, if anything, it is like for a system to undergo its
states. Nagel’s formulation is the standard one: an organism has conscious mental
states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism, something it is like
for the organism [26]. The question is whether an account of computational transitions
entails the existence of phenomenal properties, or whether such properties are being
added to the account through interpretation.

Chalmers distinguished the easy problems of consciousness, which concern the ex-
planation of functions such as discrimination, report, attention, and the control of
behavior, from the hard problem, which concerns why the performance of these func-
tions is accompanied by experience at all [9]. On this view the easy problems are
solved in the ordinary way, by specifying mechanisms, and a computational account
can in principle solve all of them, while leaving the hard problem untouched. Levine’s
earlier notion of an explanatory gap makes a related point, that even a complete
physical account of a state does not appear to make intelligible why the state is felt
as it is [22]. These positions generate Proposition 2 directly. A speciﬁcation of state
transitions is a speciﬁcation of the sort of thing that the easy problems concern, and
one who wants to say that it also yields experience must supply a further premise.

Physicalist and illusionist responses reject the framing. Dennett argued that the hard
problem is an artifact of a mistaken picture of consciousness as a special inner medium,
and that once the functions are explained, nothing remains to be explained but the
persistent illusion that something does [14]. Illusionism in its later forms holds that
phenomenal properties, as philosophers conceive them, do not exist, and that the task
is to explain why systems like us judge that they do [18]. If this is right, the demand for
a derivation of experience from computation is a demand for something that has no
object, and the question of machine consciousness reduces to the question of whether
machines have the relevant introspective machinery and the associated judgments.


                                     7

The position is serious and consistent, and it should be stated carefully. Illusionists
do not in general deny that pain or suffering exist. They deny that these states have
the intrinsic, ineffable, and private qualitative properties some philosophers ascribe
to them, and they hold that the states are real and morally important under their
functional description. Illusionism therefore does not undermine the moral standing
of humans or other animals. Its bearing on the machine case is that whether a machine
suffers becomes a question about whether it has the relevant functional organization,
and a report of distress is neither sufﬁcient evidence of it nor irrelevant to it. The
position relocates the problem more than it resolves it, and it supplies a route to
machine moral standing that does not pass through phenomenal consciousness in the
contested sense.

The strongest functionalist reply to the explanatory gap deserves a fuller statement. It
holds that the gap is a feature of the concepts in which we think about experience and
not of the phenomena, and that it is therefore compatible with the identity of conscious
states with functional or physical states [23, 29]. On this phenomenal concept strategy,
the concepts we apply to our own experiences from the inside do not reveal the
functional or physical nature of what they pick out, which produces the appearance
that no physical account could entail them even though the states are the same. If this
is right, Proposition 2 remains true as a claim about what a functional speciﬁcation
makes intelligible, while the conclusion that experience is something over and above
function does not follow. The proposition is therefore compatible with computational
functionalism being true. What it denies is that a functional speciﬁcation, without
further argument, settles which systems have experience, and the strategy is itself
silent on that point: it says that experience may be identical with some functional
organization, and does not say which organizations, or whether present systems have
the right one.

The failure of an existing computational description to explain consciousness is not a
demonstration that no computational system could be conscious. An explanatory gap
is a feature of current understanding, and it is compatible with some computational
organizations giving rise to experience in ways we lack the concepts to see. The
stronger impossibility thesis would require a necessary condition for consciousness
that computational systems cannot satisfy, and Section 13 takes up that task. What
this section supports is the weaker thesis that a computational description, however
elaborate, leaves open whether experience is present, so that the question must be
settled by additional theory and evidence.





                                     8

6. Why Behavioral Indistinguishability Is Not Ontological Identity


Turing proposed replacing the question whether machines can think with a test of
whether a machine can be told apart from a human in conversation [41]. The proposal
was a deliberate and productive operationalization, and it has been useful for decades,
but it is an operationalization of a different question. The ability to produce responses
indistinguishable from those of a conscious person establishes a property of the
interaction and of the observer’s powers of discrimination. It does not automatically
establish an identity between the underlying systems. Epistemic indistinguishability
is a relation between a system and an observer under a speciﬁed set of observations,
and ontological equivalence is a relation between two systems. Two systems can be
indistinguishable under one set of observations while differing in properties that those
observations do not measure, which is simply what it means for observations to be
limited.

This is Proposition 1, and it holds in a precise sense that can be illustrated by coun-
termodel. Put more exactly, a ﬁnite set of observations O does not ﬁx phenomenal
status across the interpretations of the bridge principle T that connect organization to
consciousness, and attribution is a function of O and T together and never of O alone.
The countermodel below illustrates this and is not needed for it. Take any ﬁnite set of
behavioral observations of a human being. A lookup table indexed on the same inputs
reproduces those observations, and the table does not have the human’s phenomenal
properties on any view that gives table lookup no experience, a view that even most
functionalists accept. The countermodel does not show that a particular large language
model resembles a lookup table, which it does not. It shows that the inference form,
from a given behavioral proﬁle to a given phenomenal proﬁle, is invalid without a
bridge principle connecting the proﬁle to the internal organization, and that the bridge
principle is exactly what is under dispute. Functionalists supply one, which is that the
behavioral proﬁle together with a certain internal organization sufﬁces. Their position
then depends on a claim about internal organization, which behavior alone cannot
establish.

The point is particularly pressing for large language models because of how they are
produced. Their training directly rewards the production of linguistic forms associated
with human understanding, reﬂection, emotion, and interpersonal competence. In
ordinary human life, ﬂuent talk about one’s feelings is a reliable sign that one has
feelings, because the talk is produced by a process that is connected to the feelings. In
a system optimized to produce text that humans would rate as natural, helpful, and
humanlike, the talk is produced by a process that is connected to the optimization
target, and the connection to any feelings is at best an additional hypothesis. A
successful performance may therefore be good evidence of learned conversational


                                     9

competence without being evidence of the subjective properties ordinarily associated
with that performance. The point can be put in the language of evidence, with the
caveat that the claim is schematic and is not a measurement. Let C be the hypothesis
that the system is conscious and r a particular report, such as a statement that it is
afraid. The evidential force of r is carried by the likelihood ratio

                                       P(r | C)
                             Λ(r) =                                                (1)                                      P(r | ¬C).

For a human speaker in a sincere ﬁrst-person context, P(r  | ¬C) is small, because
the ordinary processes that produce such reports in humans run through the states
reported, and so Λ(r) is large. The qualiﬁcation matters, since humans also report fear
when lying, acting, quoting, or dreaming, and the value of the ratio depends on how
the hypothesis and the reporting context are speciﬁed. For a system whose training
selects for text that humans would rate as natural, the training supplies an alternative
causal explanation of the report, one that does not run through the state reported.
The claim that follows is conditional, and it is not a mathematical consequence of the
training objective. To the extent that the production of r is ﬁxed by the optimization
target independently of C, the report is about equally probable under C and under
¬C, and Λ(r) approaches one. To the extent that it is not, the numerator and the
denominator may move differently, and nothing general can be said. The argument
therefore establishes a direction and a condition, and it does not establish a magnitude
or that Λ(r) equals one. It also yields a less obvious result, which is that a self-report
can become less informative about consciousness precisely because the system has
become better at producing convincing self-reports independently of consciousness.
On a theory in which reports are generated by introspective mechanisms that track
internal states, P(r | C) could remain higher than P(r | ¬C), and how far the reports
of a given model depend on its internal states rather than on the surface statistics of its
training text is an open empirical question. The conceptual point is that the reports
cannot be assigned their human evidential weight without that further investigation.
The schematic ratio should also be read with two speciﬁcations made explicit. The
hypothesis C is the presence of phenomenal experience of the kind the report describes,
and not consciousness in general, since a system could be conscious in some respect
without having the state it reports. And the ratio is properly conditioned on what
is known about the mechanism that produces the report, which may be written K,
so that the relevant quantity is Λ(r; K) = P(r | C, K)/P(r | ¬C, K). The comparison
between a human report and a model report is then a comparison between two values
of K, and the argument of this section is that the second value is not licensed to inherit
the ﬁrst.

A skeptic about the asymmetry will observe that the independent evidence available in


                                    10

the human case is itself largely behavioral and structural, and that the problem of other
minds shows that the inference to another person’s experience is never deductively
secure. This is correct, and it is why the argument does not claim certainty about
the human case. The asymmetry is one of explanatory structure. In the human case
the best explanation of a report of fear invokes states of the same kind as one’s own,
produced by a shared biology and a shared developmental history, and the analogy
supplies a reason for the inference that does not rest on behavior alone. In the artiﬁcial
case the analogy is weaker along exactly the dimensions that carried the inference,
and there is a competing explanation, the training objective, that accounts for the
report without invoking experience. The difference is not one between certainty
and uncertainty. It is a difference in how much the available evidence discriminates
between the hypotheses.

Recent work on assessing consciousness in artiﬁcial systems has recognized the difﬁ-
culty and has proposed that assessment proceed through the theories of consciousness,
deriving indicator properties from each theory and asking whether the system has
them, rather than through behavior [8]. This is a more defensible research program
than the behavioral one, and its own conclusions have been cautious. It does not use
the system’s self-reports as evidence for the system’s experiences, and it recognizes
that different theories yield different indicators, so that the verdict depends on a prior
choice among theories that is itself unsettled.


7. Agency Without an Agent


The next distinction concerns artiﬁcial agency. Robots and software agents pursue
goals, select actions, revise plans, and respond to changing environments, and these are
legitimate functional descriptions. They are supported by a long tradition of treating
purposive behavior as the behavior of systems regulated by feedback toward a target
[32], and by Dennett’s observation that the intentional stance, in which a system is
predicted by attributing beliefs and desires to it, is available and useful for any system
whose behavior is well predicted that way, thermostats included [13]. Dennett’s own
view is subtler than a predictive convenience. In his account of real patterns, beliefs
and desires are real in virtue of the predictive and explanatory patterns in which
they ﬁgure, and not in virtue of some further intrinsic essence [15]. On this view the
question whether a system has beliefs is not the question whether it has a hidden inner
ingredient, and it may have an afﬁrmative answer for systems that are not conscious.
That is compatible with the present argument, since attribution of belief in this sense is
a thesis about content and prediction and carries no thesis about experience or moral
standing.



                                    11

The distinctions that matter here are between assigned objectives and intrinsic inter-
ests, between optimization and desire, and between policy selection and deliberative
subjectivity. A thermostat regulates temperature without wanting warmth, and a
robot can navigate a building without necessarily experiencing it. In each case a goal
is speciﬁed by a designer or by a training signal, the system’s behavior is selected to
advance it, and the goal belongs to the system only in the thin sense that it appears
in the system’s speciﬁcation. An intrinsic interest, by contrast, is one the system has
independently of any speciﬁcation, in the sense that its own continued existence and
ﬂourishing are at stake for it. Whether the thin sense can grow into the thick one as
systems become more autonomous is a real question, and the thought that it requires
something like self-maintenance, a system that must keep itself going in order to
continue to be, is developed in the literature on autopoiesis and biological autonomy
[24, 39].

The discussion must also recognize that sophisticated biological agency is not reducible
to conscious deliberation. Many human actions are automatic, and many living organ-
isms exhibit goal-directed behavior without an established capacity for phenomenal
consciousness. A bacterium follows a chemical gradient, a plant orients toward light,
and a person catches a falling object before being aware of having seen it. If agency
required consciousness, these would not be cases of agency, and if consciousness
required agency, then a person unable to act would not be conscious, which is false.
Consequently neither agency nor its absence provides a simple test for consciousness.
This cuts in both directions. The presence of sophisticated goal-directed behavior in
an artifact does not settle that it has experience, although it may bear on the question
under particular theories, and the absence of free or autonomous action would not
settle that it lacks it. Proposition 4 states the limited point that can be defended:
optimization toward speciﬁed objectives does not, without further premises, establish
conscious intention.


8. Identity, Continuity, and the Manufactured Individual


The attribution of individuality to chatbots depends on a set of presentational features.
A model has a name, a conversational style, a persistent memory, a user proﬁle, and a
set of apparent preferences, and together these create a convincing impression of an
enduring interlocutor. The impression is a fact about the interface. It remains to be
shown that it corresponds to an experiencing subject, and the continuity of an interface
does not automatically establish the continuity of such a subject.

Several different things are called the model, and they come apart. There are the
weights, a ﬁxed array of numbers produced by training. There are running instances,


                                    12

each of which is a computation using those weights on some input. There are con-
versation histories, which are text that may be stored, edited, or discarded. There are
externally stored memories, which are records that a deployment retrieves and inserts
into the input. There are, ﬁnally, the ﬁctional or operational identities presented to
users, which are roles that the system is instructed or trained to play and that may
differ across products built on the same weights. A human being is a single thing that
uniﬁes all of these roles, and for that reason the ordinary concept of a person has no
need to separate them. In the artiﬁcial case they are separate, and the question which
of them, if any, is the individual has no obvious answer.

If two identical instances of a model are launched, what makes either of them an
individual? If one instance is copied mid-conversation, which continuation possesses
the original identity? If memory is deleted, has an individual suffered amnesia, or has
a data structure been modiﬁed? These puzzles resemble those of the personal identity
literature, in which ﬁssion, duplication, and gradual replacement test intuitions about
what matters in survival [28]. Parﬁt’s own conclusion was that identity is not what
matters, and that psychological continuity and connectedness are, which might be
taken to favor the artiﬁcial case, since such systems can have continuity without a
determinate identity. If Parﬁt is right, the copying puzzles point to a concept that
should be discarded and not to a deﬁciency in the artiﬁcial case, and the difﬁculty
of saying which instance is the original carries no special weight against machine
individuality. This is a fair point, and it limits what the puzzles can show. It does not
remove the question of what the connectedness is a connectedness of. On Parﬁt’s ac-
count what matters is a relation among psychological states, valued because the states
are experienced by someone or something in a continuing way, and informational
connectedness between data structures is not obviously the same relation. The puzzles
about copying are therefore puzzles about how to count experiencing subjects, and
they presuppose that there are some to count.

These questions do not prove the absence of machine individuality. They show how
much philosophical work is required before ordinary personal-identity concepts can
be applied, and the task here is to keep four notions apart. Numerical identity is the
relation of being one and the same thing. Informational continuity is the preservation
of data across time. Functional continuity is the preservation of dispositions to respond.
Phenomenal continuity is the unity of experience across time, if there is any. For a
human being the four go together so reliably that they are rarely distinguished. For
an artiﬁcial system they can be dissociated at will, by engineers, and Proposition 3
states that the ﬁrst three do not entail the fourth. A product that persists under one
name with a retrievable record has informational continuity, and perhaps functional
continuity, and whether it has any further continuity depends on whether it has
experience in the ﬁrst place.

9. The Architecture Behind the Interlocutor


A conversational interface presents a uniﬁed object. A user opens an application,
addresses a named assistant, receives a response, and returns later to continue the
exchange. The apparent unity of this interaction can obscure the distributed machin-
ery responsible for producing it. The relevant engineering is not mysterious, even
though the complete details of commercial deployments are often proprietary. Modern
language-model services commonly separate authentication, conversation storage,
request routing, model inference, safety processing, tool execution, and response
delivery into distinct components. Some deployments implement these functions as
microservices, which are independently deployed services that communicate through
deﬁned interfaces, while others combine them, and the division varies across products.
The philosophical point does not depend on one particular arrangement. The iden-
tity presented by the interface is not identical with any single computational process
responsible for producing a response.

A typical request begins when a client submits a message together with an identiﬁer
for the relevant conversation. The application retrieves the available conversational
context, which may include previous messages, summaries, user preferences, system
instructions, and externally stored information. A routing or orchestration component
constructs the input for inference, potentially selecting a model, allocating computa-
tional resources, and deciding which tools or retrieval operations are available. The
inference system processes the assembled input and produces output tokens. Those to-
kens may be streamed to the client while generation continues. The resulting messages
and associated records may then be stored for subsequent requests.

These stages need not execute on the same computer, within the same process, or even
within the same deployment region. Inference requests may be assigned to different
workers, and the same model weights may be loaded into multiple independent
serving instances. Systems may also maintain caches, persistent sessions, or stateful
execution environments for performance and continuity. Microservice architecture
therefore does not imply that every request begins from a completely empty machine.
It implies that the continuity visible to the user must be distinguished from the
organization and lifetime of the computational processes that implement it.

Two further facts about the inference step bear on the question of continuity. First, in
the common design the inference step is stateless with respect to the user. A request
arrives with its assembled context, a worker computes the response, and the worker
is then free to serve another request, from another user, with no residue of the ﬁrst
beyond whatever the operators choose to cache for performance. Second, the weights
are ﬁxed during use. A conversation does not modify the learned parameters, so



                                    14

whatever the user perceives as the assistant adapting to them is accomplished through
the context supplied with each request and not through any change to the model. In the
common request-response arrangement, no computation on behalf of the conversation
is running in the interval between messages. Processing occurs while a response
is being generated. Other deployments differ, since persistent agents, continuous
audio or video processing, recurrent-state models, long-running tool executions, and
scheduled background work all produce computation outside the narrow request-
response cycle, and in those cases that computation is also a designed process with
its own inputs and outputs. The point does not depend on which arrangement is in
use, because continuity of computation, where it exists, is not continuity of experience.
What matters is the distinction between the continuity a service presents to its user
and the persistence of any particular computational process, and that distinction holds
whether or not a given process runs continuously. These are descriptions of common
practice and not of every deployment, and they are stated at the level at which such
services are generally described.

This distinction is particularly important because a language model is not ordinarily
the whole application. The model weights specify learned computational parameters.
They do not themselves contain the complete conversational history of every user
interacting with a service. Conversation records, external memory systems, tool
results, and application policies may be managed independently. A named assistant
can consequently remain available while particular inference workers are restarted,
replaced, or reassigned. The same interface identity can survive changes in hardware,
model version, context representation, and execution environment.

It helps to separate four layers that the single name of an assistant tends to merge. At
the model layer what persists is a set of learned parameters, which establish reusable
computational dispositions and nothing more. At the inference layer what exists is a
set of activations and temporary state, which constitute one particular computation.
At the application layer what persists is history, memory, and identiﬁers, which
establish informational continuity. At the interface layer what persists is a name, a
persona, and a manner of presentation, which establish an apparent social identity.
The layers may overlap or be implemented differently in different products, and their
conceptual separation matters more than where the physical boundaries between
services happen to fall. A microservice decomposition is a way of organizing software
and is not a theory of consciousness: a distributed system can have persistent state and
coordinated, continuous processes, and a monolithic program can lack every property
that a theory of consciousness treats as relevant. The claim is therefore the narrower
one that such a decomposition makes the construction of apparent conversational unity
intelligible without requiring a uniﬁed subject, and it is not the claim that distribution
excludes experience.


                                    15

There is no engineering mystery about how such continuity can be presented. A service
can preserve records and use them to reconstruct the conditions for a subsequent
response. What remains philosophically disputed is whether any of the computational
activity involved also constitutes experience. The architectural account does not prove
that no process is conscious. It does, however, provide an independently established
explanation for the appearance of a persistent interlocutor, without requiring an
enduring experiencing subject.

The burden of explanation is consequently shifted.  It is not necessary to posit a
continuing individual in order to explain why the application remembers an earlier
conversation. The application can remember because information was stored and sub-
sequently retrieved. Anyone claiming that this informational continuity additionally
constitutes personal continuity must identify the further property and show how the
system possesses it.


10. Stored Context and the Appearance of a Continuing Self


The continuity of a chatbot is frequently described in autobiographical terms.  It
remembers an earlier conversation, recognizes a returning user, refers to previous
commitments, and may describe itself as having changed its mind. These expres-
sions invite interpretation through the ordinary psychology of human memory. Yet
conversational continuity in deployed language-model systems can be produced by
operations that are already understood in computational terms.

For an autoregressive language model, the next-token distribution can be represented
schematically as
                                Pθ(xt+1 | x1, . . . , xt),                                  (2)

where θ denotes learned parameters and x1, . . . , xt denotes the available token context.
During inference, intermediate activations and attention caches may preserve infor-
mation across successive token-generation steps. Such state is computationally real
and causally relevant. It should not be confused with an autobiographical subject, nor
should it be denied merely because it is temporary.

At the level of the application, the input context may be reconstructed from stored
records.  Let Hn denote the available history before interaction n, let Mn denote
externally maintained memory, and let Sn denote governing instructions and other
supplied context. A simpliﬁed interaction can be represented as

                         Yn ∼Pθ( · | Xn, Hn, Mn, Sn),                              (3)

where Xn is the new user input and Yn is the generated response, drawn from a


                                    16

distribution because sampling is ordinarily stochastic. The application may then
update its records according to

                     (Hn+1, Mn+1) = U(Hn, Mn, Xn, Yn, En),                       (4)

where En stands for external inﬂuences on the update, such as retrieval policies, com-
pression of older material, operator or human intervention, and elapsed time. These
expressions describe a class of possible implementations, not the internal speciﬁcation
of any particular commercial product. Their purpose is to show how a continuing con-
versation can be generated through the persistence and transformation of information
across separate inference operations.

Nothing in this arrangement requires the system to have remained phenomenally
present during the interval between interactions. A conversation may resume after
minutes or months because the application retains enough information to construct an
appropriate continuation. A previous exchange may be summarized, truncated, or
selectively retrieved. What appears as recollection may be the processing of a record
that the current inference operation did not itself produce.

This is not equivalent to saying that the system has no memory. In computer science,
persistent storage and context-dependent state are genuine forms of memory. The
distinction concerns what follows from their existence. The possession of stored
information does not entail the recollective experience ordinarily associated with
human autobiographical memory.

The distinction also exposes an ambiguity in claims about a chatbot’s identity.  If
a service changes the model weights while preserving the conversation record, the
user may encounter what appears to be the same assistant. If the service preserves
the weights but discards the record, the assistant may appear to have forgotten its
past. If the record is copied into two independent sessions, both continuations may
produce equally convincing claims to the same history. These outcomes are intelligible
as consequences of information management, but they do not establish how many
experiencing subjects, if any, are present.

The argument is not that discontinuous computation could never support conscious-
ness. Biological consciousness itself is interrupted by sleep, anesthesia, and other
changes in functional organization, and theories of personal identity differ about what
persists through such interruptions. The narrower claim is that the observed continuity
of the conversational interface has a sufﬁcient engineering explanation that does not
establish phenomenal continuity.

A chatbot’s apparent biography is therefore not independent evidence of an experi-
encing individual. It is an output conditioned on information made available to the


                                    17

system. Whether that output corresponds to a subject is a further question, not one
answered by the successful preservation of the conversation.


11. Training on Human Expression and the Production of Apparent
    Mentality


The architecture explains how a conversational interface can maintain continuity
without establishing the persistence of an experiencing subject. The training process
explains why the resulting responses so readily resemble the expressions of one.
Contemporary language models acquire much of their linguistic competence from
large collections of human-produced material, supplemented in various systems by
synthetic data, supervised examples, preference optimization, and other forms of
post-training. These processes are designed to improve the production of useful,
appropriate, and contextually convincing responses.

Human writing contains more than descriptions of external facts. It contains reports
of feelings, declarations of intention, confessions, autobiographical narratives, moral
judgments, expressions of sympathy, and conversations between people who under-
stand themselves as experiencing subjects. A model trained to predict or generate
language from such material learns statistical and structural regularities associated
with these forms of expression. It can reproduce their organization without the train-
ing procedure establishing that it possesses the experiences ordinarily associated with
them.

The distinction can be stated without assuming that language modeling is merely the
memorization of sentences. Modern models can generalize, combine information,
solve problems, and generate novel expressions. The argument does not require
denying these capabilities.  It requires distinguishing the capacity to construct an
appropriate expression from the possession of the psychological state that expression
conventionally reports.

Post-training strengthens the effect. Human annotators or evaluators may compare
candidate responses according to criteria such as helpfulness, correctness, politeness,
safety, coherence, and responsiveness to the user’s circumstances. Preference models
or other optimization procedures can then increase the probability of outputs satisfying
those criteria. Not every model uses the same training pipeline, and some systems
rely on AI-generated feedback or alternative optimization methods. Nevertheless, the
common feature is that external judgments shape the system’s observable behavior.

Consider a response that expresses sympathy. The training process may favor lan-
guage that acknowledges distress, avoids inappropriate dismissal, and offers relevant


                                    18

assistance. The resulting expression can be socially appropriate and practically useful.
Its appropriateness does not demonstrate that the system experiences sympathy. The
relevant distinction is between a behavioral disposition acquired through optimization
and the subjective state that similar behavior may express in a human being.

This creates a particular evidentiary difﬁculty. The training data contains linguistic
evidence of human experience, while the training procedure rewards the reproduc-
tion of forms associated with successful human communication. Consequently, the
presence of those forms in model output cannot be treated as independent evidence
that the model possesses the corresponding experiences. The very process that makes
the response convincing supplies an alternative explanation for its production. The
likelihood analysis of Section 6 applies directly, since the training process supplies the
alternative causal explanation of the report on which that analysis turns.

Ted Chiang has argued along related lines that a chatbot exchange is better understood
as the continuation of a document than as a conversation between two parties, so
that the conversational character is a product of text completion, and that attributing
consciousness or moral agency to such systems displaces responsibility from the com-
panies that build them [10]. His conclusion concerns contemporary language models
and is stated more ﬁrmly than the propositions defended here. The present essay
adopts the narrower point that the mechanism producing a convincing conversational
character does not itself establish the phenomenal status of that character, and it notes
that the responsibility-displacement concern is the one developed above as agentive
responsibility displacement.

The distinction becomes especially important when the model generates ﬁrst-person
expressions. Statements such as “I understand,” “I remember,” “I want,” and “I am
uncomfortable” have familiar psychological interpretations when uttered by human
beings. In an artiﬁcial conversational system, their production may be explained by
learned linguistic regularities, post-training preferences, governing instructions, and
available context. The grammatical ﬁrst person is not evidence of a metaphysical ﬁrst
person.

There is a further complication. Training on human evaluations can reward responses
that preserve the impression of a stable, considerate, and self-consistent personality.
Such consistency is useful for interaction, but it can also be mistaken for evidence of an
underlying character. The model appears to possess enduring commitments because
the system has been optimized to produce responses consistent with those commit-
ments. A designed behavioral regularity is thereby interpreted as a psychological
property.

None of this establishes that learning from human language is incompatible with
consciousness. Human beings also learn expressions of emotion, social roles, and


                                    19

moral vocabulary through interaction with other people. The difference is that human
attribution is supported by independent biological, developmental, and physiological
evidence, whereas the artiﬁcial case requires an account of how its computational
processes instantiate the relevant properties. Training on human expression does not
provide that account merely by producing increasingly persuasive expressions.

The architecture and the training process therefore explain complementary aspects of
the same appearance. Distributed application components and stored context produce
the continuity of an interlocutor. Learned linguistic structure and behavioral opti-
mization produce the recognizable expressions of mentality. Together they can create
the impression of a persistent, responsive, emotionally competent individual. The
impression is explicable through known engineering operations. Whether anything
further is present remains a separate ontological question, and it cannot be answered
by treating the success of the impression as evidence of its own authenticity.


12. Embodiment Is Not Consciousness


Robotics introduces a further source of confusion, which is physical embodiment. A
robot may have cameras, tactile sensors, actuators, proprioceptive systems, spatial
maps, and adaptive control policies. These capabilities establish sensorimotor organi-
zation. They do not by themselves establish subjective awareness, and the inference
from one to the other repeats at the level of the body the inference from linguistic
competence to understanding.

The embodied and enactive traditions have argued that cognition is constituted by
the dynamic coupling of an organism with its environment, and not by computations
performed on internal representations [43, 39]. Predictive processing accounts hold
that perception and action are two aspects of the minimization of prediction error, and
a number of authors have connected this to consciousness by way of the regulation of
the body’s internal state, so that the felt quality of experience is rooted in the organism’s
need to stay alive [37, 11]. These views have a common structural feature that matters
here. They place the source of experience in biological regulation, in the fact that for a
living system certain states are better or worse for it, and this is not a property that a
robot acquires by having sensors and motors. A robot with a battery that must be kept
charged has a regulation problem in a real sense, since its continued operation depends
on maintaining certain physical conditions, and this dependence does not become
unreal because a designer arranged it. Evolution likewise produced the regulatory
mechanisms of organisms without conferring intrinsic interests by that fact alone,
so the origin of a system’s goals is not the relevant distinction. The more defensible
distinction concerns the constitutive organization of the goal-directed activity. In


                                    20

an autopoietic system the regulatory activity continuously produces and maintains
the very components and conditions that constitute the system, so that the system
exists only as long as the activity continues, whereas the maintenance procedures
of a machine preserve an externally speciﬁed functional organization realized in
separately manufactured parts. Whether this difference matters for experience is
again a disputed question, and these theories supply candidate reasons why it might,
without establishing that it does.

Humanoid appearance, expressive movement, and responsive speech intensify an-
thropomorphic attribution, and this effect is well documented and independent of
the system’s internal organization. A machine that withdraws its hand from a hot
surface may be implementing a protective control policy. That behavior alone does
not establish pain, and the inference to pain is tempting because the observer has
learned the category of withdrawal behavior from encounters with living organisms,
for which the inference is generally warranted. The categories that observers apply to
mechanical responses were acquired in a world in which moving, responsive things
were almost always alive, and the habits of attribution that this world produced do
not carry over automatically to artifacts that were engineered to trigger them.

The point applies with particular force to conversational services, which lack embod-
iment in the sense that the theories above treat as relevant. A deployed text-based
chatbot has no sensorimotor loop with a physical environment, since its input is text,
ﬁles, or tool results supplied through an interface, and its output is text. Multimodal
models that process live audio, images, or video, and models connected to robotic
control systems, do have richer inputs and outputs, and for them the more precise
claim is that they lack organismic embodiment, meaning the metabolic, interoceptive,
self-producing, and homeostatic organization that the theories above treat as relevant,
and not that they lack sensors. The hardware on which inference runs is not a body to
which the system’s states are regulatively coupled, because the same weights can be
served from many machines interchangeably, and no process monitors or maintains
the viability of any particular instance or of the model as such. Nothing about the
service depends on the system keeping itself in existence, and the maintenance of the
infrastructure is carried out by its operators. This does not settle whether embodiment
is necessary for experience, which Section 13 treats as open. It does mean that the
considerations from biological regulation that motivate the embodied theories give
no support to the attribution in the case of text-based services. Agentic deployments
that connect a model to tools, browsers, or robot bodies change the picture in some
respects, and the earlier considerations about robots apply to them.
