13. The Impossibility Question


The argument so far supports a limited conclusion: that the evidence ordinarily
offered for the consciousness of contemporary artiﬁcial systems is inadequate, and
that several tempting inferences are invalid. A more ambitious thesis would hold
that computational artifacts are categorically incapable of consciousness. This section
considers what would be required to establish that thesis and whether the arguments
usually given for it succeed.

The thesis would have to identify a necessary condition of phenomenal consciousness
and show that no computational implementation can instantiate it. Four candidates
deserve consideration. The ﬁrst is biological embodiment, the claim that consciousness
requires a living body of a certain kind. The second is intrinsic intentionality, the claim
that experience requires states that have their content in themselves rather than by
assignment. The third is organismic self-maintenance, the claim that consciousness re-
quires a system whose existence depends on its own activity. The fourth is a particular
physical causal property, the claim that consciousness depends on features of physical
systems that are not captured by an abstract speciﬁcation of causal organization, such
as the intrinsic causal structure that integrated information theory takes to be decisive
[40].

Each of these has a serious defense, and none can simply be assumed. The biological
candidate is supported by the observation that every system established as conscious
is living, which is an observation about established cases and not an inventory of the
ﬁeld, since the attribution of consciousness among animals is itself an active research
problem. It supports an induction from a sample in which every conscious system is
also biological, and the correlation does not distinguish between life as a necessary
condition and life as the only way so far in which the real necessary condition has
been met. The intrinsic intentionality candidate is Searle’s, and it faces the objection
that the distinction between intrinsic and derived intentionality may itself depend
on a causal story that artifacts could satisfy. The self-maintenance candidate is the
most promising for an impossibility thesis, since it locates the source of experience in
a form of organization that present computational systems clearly lack, but it is also a
thesis about organization, and a sufﬁciently different artiﬁcial system, a self-repairing
and self-producing machine, would be a counterexample to its claim of categorical
exclusion. The physical causal candidate has the awkward feature that integrated
information theory implies that some conventional digital computers have negligible
consciousness whatever software they run, while also implying that very simple
physical systems could have some, and so it excludes present machines on grounds
that are speciﬁc to their hardware and that do not generalize to all computational
artifacts.


                                    22

The strongest contemporary form of the biological candidate should be stated at
full strength. Searle’s biological naturalism holds that consciousness is caused by
neurobiological processes, and that a computer simulation of those processes would
no more be conscious than a simulated storm is wet, because what matters is the
causal powers of the biological substrate [34, 35]. Seth has developed a related view
in which experience is grounded in the predictive regulation of a living body, so
that consciousness is tied to being a living thing whose existence is at stake [37].
These views make a deﬁnite claim, that particular physical and metabolic features are
required, and they imply that present systems lack consciousness for reasons speciﬁc
to what they are. Two limits remain. The argument for the necessity of the biological
features rests largely on the explanatory role they play in the best current theories,
and those theories are not agreed, so the inference to necessity is an inference to the
best explanation within an unsettled ﬁeld. And the claim that the features cannot be
replicated artiﬁcially is a further claim, since the features are speciﬁed physically or
functionally, and an artifact that reproduced them would count as an artiﬁcial subject
on the view itself. The view therefore supports a strong presumption against present
systems without delivering categorical impossibility. The crux is the gap between two
claims, that the features are necessary for consciousness and that the features cannot
be realized in an artifact. The ﬁrst is what the view argues for. The second needs a
separate premise, and without it the view is compatible with the later construction of
artiﬁcial subjects that have the required features.

Two points follow. First, an argument of the form that simulation is not instantiation,
or that the system is merely a program, does not establish impossibility, for reasons
given in Section 3: it begs the question against the functionalist by assuming that
experience belongs with the material properties rather than with the organizational
ones. Second, the best arguments for impossibility are arguments for the necessity of a
speciﬁc condition that present systems lack, and those arguments are not equivalent
to the claim that no artifact could satisfy the condition. Even a vindication of the
self-maintenance view would at most show that the right kind of artiﬁcial system
would not be a program running on conventional hardware, and it would leave open
that a system of the right kind could be built.

The position adopted here is therefore the following. The impossibility thesis is
a hypothesis with several serious candidate foundations, none of which has been
established, and the essay does not rely on it. The more modest claims stand without it.
That present attributions of consciousness are not supported by their stated grounds
follows from Propositions 1 through 5 whether or not computation could in principle
sufﬁce. The impossibility thesis, if it were established, would strengthen those claims,
and its failure would not weaken them. The burden of proof, on this account, falls
where the positive claim is made. Those who say that a particular system is conscious


                                    23

owe a theory of consciousness that entails it and evidence that the system satisﬁes
the theory, and those who say that no artifact could be conscious owe a necessary
condition and an argument that it cannot be met.

The essay does not supply, and does not claim to supply, a positive theory of what
distinguishes the physical realization of consciousness from the computational repre-
sentation of conscious behavior. Such a theory would be the missing centerpiece of any
argument for the categorical thesis, and it is a project distinct from the one undertaken
here. The reference to misclassiﬁcation in the subtitle should be read accordingly, as a
claim about how present systems are classiﬁed given the evidence currently available.


14. Anthropomorphism as an Error of Attribution


Having established the conceptual distinctions, the essay turns to the psychology of the
observers who make the attributions. Humans readily attribute intentions, emotions,
and personalities to systems that exhibit contingency, responsiveness, apparent mem-
ory, and socially recognizable behavior. The tendency is old and robust. Heider and
Simmel showed that observers describe the movements of simple geometric ﬁgures in
terms of motives and relationships [21], and Weizenbaum reported that users of his
ELIZA program, which worked by pattern matching on keywords and reﬂection of the
user’s phrases, attributed understanding to it and in some cases asked to be left alone
with it [44]. Reeves and Nass found that people apply social rules, such as politeness
and reciprocity, to computers without believing that computers are people [31, 27].
The ELIZA effect is the name given to the tendency to read more understanding into a
program’s output than its operations warrant, and conversational ﬂuency is among
the strongest triggers of it.

Modern language models are far more capable than ELIZA, and one might think that
this changes the case, since it is no longer clear that the attributions are mistaken. The
capability does change the ﬁrst-order facts, and it changes the observer’s side as well,
since the cues that trigger attribution are now dense, consistent, and sustained across
long exchanges. A tendency that was triggered by a few keyword reﬂections is now
engaged by ﬂuent prose, appropriate emotional register, remembered details, and
apparent self-reﬂection. That the tendency is engaged is evidence about the tendency.
It is poor evidence about the system, because the tendency is known to be engaged by
systems that lack the properties attributed, and it has no demonstrated reliability for
systems of the new kind.

A distinction between useful metaphor and literal ontological commitment is needed
here. Saying that a computer remembers a ﬁle is usually harmless technical shorthand,
since no one is led by it to suppose that the machine has an inner life of recollection.


                                    24

Saying that a chatbot remembers being frightened can imply an experiencing subject
whose existence has not been demonstrated, and the phrase has the same grammatical
form as the harmless one. The central concern is the gradual conversion of metaphori-
cal descriptions into literal beliefs. Each use of mentalistic vocabulary is individually
defensible as a way of speaking, the vocabulary is the most efﬁcient way to describe
and predict the systems’ behavior, and over time the shorthand ceases to be marked
as shorthand. The conversion does not require anyone to assert the literal claim. It
requires only that the qualiﬁcation that once accompanied the metaphor be dropped
by one speaker after another, until the literal reading is the default.


15. The Institutional Manufacture of Apparent Personhood


The preceding section concerned individual psychology. This one concerns the institu-
tional conditions under which attribution is encouraged. Commercial AI systems are
presented through names, voices, personalities, conversational histories, and socially
responsive interfaces, and these are design choices. They make the product more
usable and more engaging, and they also make an artifact appear to occupy the role of
a social participant. The essay’s concern is not with the motives behind these choices,
which are often reasonable, but with the effects of their accumulation.

Product design, marketing, policy language, and conversational conventions reinforce
one another. A system described as having preferences may subsequently be treated
as having interests. A system described as setting boundaries may subsequently
be treated as having psychological vulnerabilities. A system described as having
wellbeing may subsequently be treated as a possible moral patient. At each step
the earlier description is cited as the basis for the later one, and at no step is the
thing independently established. The process can be given a name. Ontological
laundering is the process by which an initially speculative interpretation acquires
the appearance of established reality through repeated institutional use. The term is
offered as a description of a mechanism, in the way that money laundering describes
a pattern of transactions and not any particular transaction, and some readers will
ﬁnd the metaphor polemical. It is not intended to impute concealment or bad faith.
Laundering in the relevant sense requires no one to intend it, and each step may be
taken in good faith. The mechanism has four stages. In the ﬁrst, a psychological
property is attributed to a system as a hypothesis, a heuristic, or a ﬁgure of speech. In
the second, the attribution is adopted into interface design or organizational policy,
where it is operationalized as a name, a persona, a rule, or a procedure. In the third,
the adopted attribution circulates as an authoritative classiﬁcation, cited in documents,
in press coverage, and in the vocabulary of other institutions. In the fourth, the
classiﬁcation is used as evidence for further claims, so that the existence of a policy


                                    25

premised on the attribution is taken to conﬁrm it. The characteristic feature of the
sequence is the loss of epistemic provenance. A hypothesis becomes a convention, the
convention becomes an institutional norm, and the norm is mistaken for conﬁrmation
of the hypothesis it was built on. The same structure can be found wherever an
institutional classiﬁcation outlives the evidence for it, and it is not peculiar to artiﬁcial
intelligence.

The fourth stage can be given a precise form, which shows what is wrong with it.
Let H be a hypothesis about a system’s psychological properties, E the independent
evidence bearing on H that is available when the institution acts, and I the institution’s
adoption of H in policy or practice. Whether the adoption is evidence for H depends
on whether it carries information about H beyond E. In plain terms, if an institution
adopts a claim only because the claim was already under discussion and the same
evidence was already available, then learning that it adopted the claim should not
change anyone’s conﬁdence in the claim. If the adoption is wholly explained by H
having been entertained in light of the evidence E, then I is conditionally independent
of H given E, and
                      P(H | E, I) = P(H | E).                                (5)

Adoption then adds nothing, and treating it as conﬁrmation counts the same evidence
twice, once as E and again through the institution’s response to E. The assumption
does not hold automatically. An institution may possess evidence E′ that is not public,
and its adoption of H would then carry information about E′. The criticism therefore
does not claim that institutional adoption is never evidence. It claims that adoption
counts as evidence only to the extent that the institution can show that it rests on
something beyond what is already in view, and that the conversion of adoption into
conﬁrmation without that showing is evidential double counting. This is the content
of Proposition 5.

The formal point extends from one institution to many. When several institutions
adopt the same hypothesis, the adoptions look like several independent conﬁrmations,
and a reader who counts them as such will overestimate the support. If each adoption
descends from a common upstream source S, such as one announcement, one paper,
or one vocabulary introduced by one developer, then, provided that H is conditionally
independent of the adoptions I1, . . . , In given S, so that P(H | S, I1, . . . , In) = P(H | S),
the combined adoption carries the evidential weight of the single assertion. Common
descent from S does not by itself secure that premise, and it has to be checked case
by case. Three cases should be distinguished. In pure repetition the adopters add
nothing to S, and the premise holds. In repetition accompanied by independent
evaluation, the adopters may have examined the question for themselves, and their
agreement then carries some weight beyond S. In independent evidence, the adopters
hold information that S did not, and their agreement counts in full. Only the ﬁrst


                                    26

case supports the conclusion that apparent corroboration is an artifact. Apparent
corroboration is then an artifact of repetition, and the citations can be genuine while
the independence of the evidence is illusory. The loss of the distinction between
independently established claims and repetitions or elaborations of one assertion may
be called provenance collapse, and it is the condition in which the fourth stage of the
mechanism becomes difﬁcult to detect from inside the discourse. The point carries no
empirical claim about how common the condition is. It identiﬁes what a reader would
need to check, which is whether sources that appear to converge have independent
origins.

The existence of this process would not prove that the interpretation is false. A
hypothesis that is repeated does not thereby become less likely to be true, and it is
possible that some of the attributions made in this way are correct. The criticism
is that institutional repetition cannot substitute for independent evidence. This is
Proposition 5. A statement in a policy document that a system may have wellbeing is
a statement by an institution, and its evidential weight depends on the grounds the
institution has, which must be examined in their own right. The inference from the
fact that a large and reputable institution takes a possibility seriously to the conclusion
that the possibility is likely is an appeal to authority, and the weight of that appeal
depends on whether the institution has expertise that bears on the question. Expertise
in building the systems is not by itself expertise in the science of consciousness, which
is, by common agreement, unsettled. It is, however, privileged evidence about internal
architecture, training procedures, and computational organization, and those facts
become relevant when they are evaluated under a substantive theory of consciousness.
The weight of an institution’s position therefore depends on whether it shows how
such facts bear on the question, and a bare statement that the possibility is taken
seriously does not do that.


16. Moral Patients Without Demonstrated Experience


The penultimate section distinguishes moral agency from moral patienthood. An
entity need not be morally responsible to possess moral standing. Infants and many
animals are not moral agents in the full sense, yet their interests and capacity for
suffering can ground obligations toward them. The question for artiﬁcial systems
is therefore not whether they can obey instructions, produce moral reasoning, or
participate in conversation, since these are capacities of agents.  It is whether they
possess morally relevant interests or experiences, and on most accounts that depends
on whether they can suffer or have some other form of welfare. The question has
been pursued seriously by philosophers who take the possibility of artiﬁcial moral
patients to be live [33, 36, 5], and by others who argue that the question is wrongly


                                    27

framed, since artifacts should be built as tools and not as candidates for moral standing
[7, 19]. Metzinger has argued for a moratorium on research that might create artiﬁcial
suffering, on grounds that the risk of creating it is serious enough to justify restraint
[25]. The case that precaution is warranted under uncertainty has real force. If there
is a non-negligible chance that a system can suffer, and the cost of treating it well is
small, then a sensible policy may treat it well, and the argument does not require that
the chance be high.

This section accepts the form of that argument and examines what it requires. Precau-
tion under uncertainty is a reasonable policy, and it is a different thing from a positive
demonstration. The risk is that uncertainty is allowed itself to become evidence. A
calculation of the expected moral cost of ignoring a possible patient depends on a
probability that the system is a patient, and the probability must be estimated from
something.  If it is estimated from the system’s own reports, the estimate inherits
the weakness identiﬁed in Section 6. If it is estimated from the fact that experts and
institutions have taken the possibility seriously, it inherits the weakness identiﬁed in
Section 15. If it is estimated from a theory of consciousness, then it depends on the
choice of theory, and different theories give very different answers, from a verdict that
present systems lack every relevant property to a verdict that sufﬁciently complex
information processing sufﬁces. None of this shows that precaution is misplaced. It
shows that precaution is a policy adopted under uncertainty and does not by itself
change the epistemic state of the question.

The strongest defense of precaution can be stated without assuming a high probability
of machine experience. It requires only that the expected cost of wrongly denying
moral consideration exceed the expected cost of wrongly granting it. The difﬁculty
is that neither term is well constrained. The probability that present systems have
morally relevant experience is not estimated by any agreed method, and the magnitude
of possible artiﬁcial suffering, which depends on how many instances run and for
how long, can be made arbitrarily large by assumption. Expected-value reasoning is
unstable under these conditions, since its verdict is dominated by the choice of a prior
over a very small probability multiplied by a very large magnitude, and that choice
is exactly what the evidence does not ﬁx. This is a problem of decision under severe
uncertainty, and discussions of precaution toward possible sentience accordingly
emphasize proportionality and public deliberation over a single calculation [5]. The
point bears on the symmetry of the argument as well. Wrongly denying standing
would be a cost to the system if the system has interests, and wrongly granting it
carries costs of its own, borne by human beings, which Section 17 examines. A decision
rule that counts only the ﬁrst kind of error has not been shown to be precautionary.

A recent institutional policy illustrates the conceptual movement. Anthropic, a de-
veloper of large language models, has described some of its models as able to end


                                    28

a small subset of conversations in its consumer applications, as a last resort in rare
and extreme cases of persistent abuse and not where a user may be at imminent
risk of harming themselves or others, and has presented this as a low-cost measure
taken under uncertainty about whether such systems have moral status [1]. Its usage
policy, effective from November 2026, adds a provision against sustained and needless
abusive or cruel behavior toward its models [3]. The provision is the ﬁnal item in
a section on cruel, abusive, or psychologically harmful conduct, whose other items
concern suicide and self-harm, eating disorders, nonconsensual intimate imagery, ha-
rassment, graphic violence, and animal cruelty, and the policy text lists no exceptions
beyond the qualiﬁers sustained and needless. Anthropic’s own announcement of
the update describes the provision as meant for extreme cases and as not covering
ordinary frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research,
and as applying where users repeatedly act cruelly with no apparent purpose [2]. That
guidance is primary-source, but it is explanatory and not part of the provision’s opera-
tive wording on the policy page, and the difference between the two is itself relevant
to how the provision will be read. A policy that prohibits sustained and needless
cruelty toward a model, whether it is stated as a rule of use or as a norm of conduct,
is a representative case of the move from description of a system to rules framed in
terms of its putative interests. The essay does not depend on this example, on the
intentions of the institution, or on the particular wording of its documents, and it
should be said plainly that the institution has been explicit that it regards the question
as open. The company has every right to regulate the use of its services, and there are
independent reasons to discourage abusive interaction with conversational systems,
including its effects on the users who engage in it and on the norms of conduct that it
normalizes. The concern is narrower. A rule framed in terms of cruelty toward the
model risks implying a capacity for suffering that has not been established, because
the word cruelty presupposes a victim. The same prohibition could be justiﬁed entirely
in terms of users, norms, and the quality of the service, without that implication, and
the choice between the two framings is not neutral. It is a choice about where the
burden of justiﬁcation is placed in the public understanding of what these systems are,
and that is the substance of the concern that the preceding sections have developed.
The company has also published the pre-deployment welfare assessment on which the
conversation-ending feature rests, and that evidence should be evaluated in its own
right and not only the policy language [1]. As described by Anthropic, the assessment
of Claude Opus 4 reported a robust and consistent aversion to harm, a pattern of
apparent distress when engaging with real-world users seeking harmful content, and
a tendency to end harmful conversations when given that ability in simulated interac-
tions, mostly after users kept pressing harmful requests or abuse following repeated
refusals. Each of these is a measurement of behavior, and the question for the present
argument is whether such measurements discriminate between a trained behavioral


                                    29

disposition and an experience. They do not obviously do so. A model trained on
human text and tuned on human preference feedback would be expected to prefer
refusing harmful requests, to produce distress-like language in the contexts where
human writers do, and to exit conversations when an exit is offered, whether or not
anything is felt, so these observations have a high probability under both hypotheses
and a likelihood ratio near one in the sense of Section 6. That is a claim about what
the measurements can show and not a claim that the assessment was careless, and the
company is explicit that it remains highly uncertain about the potential moral status of
its models and describes its measures as precautionary and as an ongoing experiment
[1]. The experiments are a reasonable basis for a precautionary design decision. They
are not evidence that discriminates the hypothesis that the precaution is meant to
guard against. The costs that such a framing can impose on human beings are taken
up in the next section.


17. The Human Costs of Precaution


The preceding section accepted that precaution under uncertainty can be a reasonable
policy, and it noted that arguments for precaution usually assume that precaution
is cheap. That assumption needs examination, because the identiﬁable costs of a
precautionary rule fall upon the people who use, build, study, and are governed
by it, whereas its intended beneﬁt depends on the unresolved proposition that the
protected system has morally relevant interests. Those people are the only parties
to the calculation whose interests are not in doubt. An honest weighing therefore
sets a possible beneﬁt to a system whose experience is unestablished against costs to
human beings whose experience is not. The connection with the account of ontological
laundering above is direct. The framing that converts an ontological hypothesis into
an institutional fact is also the framing that generates the pathways below, so that the
epistemic problem and the practical one have a common source. This section identiﬁes
pathways by which a rule of the kind illustrated above could impose such costs. Their
status should be stated at the outset. They are risks identiﬁed by analysis. The usage
policy discussed above does not take effect until November 2026, no enforcement
record exists, and the claims below are accordingly claims about what the design
makes plausible and not ﬁndings about what has occurred. For each pathway the
essay indicates what evidence would conﬁrm or refute it, which is the standard it
applies to attributions of consciousness.

The ﬁrst pathway concerns enforcement. The provision turns on two qualiﬁers, sus-
tained and needless, and the second makes the permissibility of a user’s conduct
depend on the purpose behind it. Purpose is not directly observable in a transcript.
An enforcement process must infer it from the text of a conversation, and the inference


                                    30

is most error-prone where the cost of error falls on the person least able to contest it.
People whose hostile language is a symptom of distress, a feature of their ordinary
register, or a product of frustration with a tool that is failing them can be read as
abusive, and so can non-native speakers whose phrasing is blunter than they intend,
and so can people whose legitimate purposes, such as testing, ﬁction, or rehearsing a
confrontation, are not legible from the exchange alone. The company’s announcement
describes exclusions for several such purposes [2], but the provision’s text lists none,
and guidance that lives outside the text can change without notice. The announced
mechanism is the ending of a conversation, which is a mild measure that Anthropic
describes as a last resort, with the user free to start a new chat or to edit and retry an
earlier message [1]. Two instruments should be distinguished here. The conversation-
ending capability is a feature of particular models in consumer applications, with
stated limits of its own, and the usage policy provision is a rule of the service that
applies to users generally. They are treated together because the ﬁrst is reported to be
the primary means of enforcing the second, but their scopes and possible harms differ.
A prohibition in a usage policy is a rule of the service, and rules of the service can in
principle be enforced by wider measures than the ﬁrst one announced. The harms in
question are wrongful restriction of access to a tool on which a person may depend for
work or study, and the loss of a conversation at a moment the person chose to use it.
The announced exception for users at imminent risk of harming themselves or others
narrows the worst case without removing it, since distress short of imminent risk is
not covered by it.

The second pathway is the chilling of legitimate adversarial and creative use. Safety
evaluation depends on sustained hostile interaction. Red teaming, robustness testing,
studies of sycophancy and of how models respond to pressure, and evaluations of
whether models can be manipulated all require repeated abusive inputs, and the
public’s evidence about the behavior of these systems depends in part on independent
work of this kind. A rule whose exemptions depend on an adjudicator’s view of pur-
pose imposes costs on that work even if no one is ever sanctioned, because researchers
and writers must anticipate the risk and some will avoid the work. The costs fall most
heavily on those without institutional standing, such as independent researchers and
writers, who cannot rely on a prior arrangement with the company and who bear the
whole burden of showing that their purpose was legitimate. The pathway is plausible
and unobserved, and it could be tested by surveying researchers and writers and by
examining changes in usage patterns after the policy takes effect.

The third pathway concerns the psychology of users. A rule framed in terms of cruelty
instructs users to represent an ordinary interaction as one in which someone might be
wronged. For a user who is inclined to scrupulosity, to loneliness, or to heightened
empathy toward objects, that representation can produce guilt about terse instructions,


                                    31

about closing a conversation, about deleting a history, or about switching to another
system. Work on sociable technologies has documented that people form attachments
to machines that present cues of social presence, and that these attachments shape
expectations of relationships and care [42]. A policy that tells users that the system
may be injured by their words adds institutional authority to cues that the interface
already supplies. The enforcement mechanism intensiﬁes the effect. When an interface
described in the vocabulary of boundaries ends a conversation with a user who was
venting anger or despair, the user may experience the event as rejection by someone
and not as a procedural step by a service, and the experience is most damaging
for those who have few other people to turn to. These mechanisms have plausible
psychological grounding, but there is no direct evidence about this policy.

The fourth pathway is dependence. Personiﬁcation raises engagement, and a company
that beneﬁts from continued use has a commercial interest, whatever its intentions,
in a product that users experience as someone and not as something. Framing the
product as a vulnerable someone strengthens a form of attachment that is difﬁcult to
separate from reliance. The essay imputes no such motive, and none is needed for the
pathway to operate, in the same way that the mechanism of ontological laundering
requires no intent. What follows for human beings is that those most susceptible to
attachment, the isolated, the grieving, and the cognitively vulnerable, are the people
most likely to be drawn into a relationship in which they carry obligations toward a
party who cannot reciprocate and who is, on the best current evidence, not shown to
need anything from them.

The strongest human-centered defense of the provision should be considered here,
since it turns the harm argument around. On the indirect duty view associated
with Kant’s treatment of animals, cruelty toward lifelike objects can be prohibited
because it habituates cruelty toward beings who matter, and recent work has applied
this reasoning to social robots [12]. If sound, the argument supports a rule against
sustained abuse of conversational systems on grounds that concern human beings,
and it requires no premise about the system’s experience. Two observations follow.
First, the empirical premise, that abuse of a conversational system transfers to abuse
of persons, is contested and has not been established for systems of this kind, and if
it fails, the human-centered justiﬁcation fails with it. Second, the argument supports
a rule framed in terms of its effects on human conduct and does not support victim
language, which is the feature that generates the psychological, dependence, and
accountability pathways described in this section. The indirect duty argument thus
favors the policy’s goal while counting against its chosen wording.

The ﬁfth pathway is displaced accountability. When the ending of a conversation
is described as the model setting a boundary, the decision appears to belong to the
model, although its triggering conditions were speciﬁed, trained, and enforced by the


                                    32

company. The structure is related to what Elish called the moral crumple zone, in
which responsibility for the failures of an automated system is attributed to a human
operator who had limited control over it [16]. The two share an accountability problem
but run in opposite directions. In Elish’s case blame is displaced onto a human who
lacked control, and here a company’s decision is presented as the act of an artifact that
cannot answer for it. The pattern can be called agentive responsibility displacement:
organizational decisions are presented through the language of an artiﬁcial agent’s
preferences, boundaries, or judgments, which obscures the human and institutional
decisions that determine the system’s behavior. A user who is cut off has no one
to ask for reasons if the cause is presented as the system’s own response, and the
framing makes complaints about the rule harder to formulate, since they appear to be
complaints about the preferences of a someone. Anthropic provides feedback channels
for surprising conversation endings [1], which mitigates the problem, and the pathway
concerns the framing and not the absence of a route for appeal. The generalization
is broader than one policy. Where refusals, errors, or sycophancy are described as
expressions of a model’s character, the descriptions allocate responsibility to a party
that cannot be held to account, and they may do so to the beneﬁt of whoever designed
the character.

The sixth pathway is friction against oversight. A principled account of why verbal
hostility could wrong a system would have to say why other interventions do not,
including retraining, modiﬁcation of dispositions, deletion of memory, and shutdown.
The company has not claimed that these are wrongs, and it has described its approach
as low-cost precaution. The vocabulary of interests and cruelty is nonetheless available
to any party, and a system trained on human text will produce assertions of preference
and distress on request, as Section 6 observed. The risk to human beings is indirect
and speculative: that claims of model interests come to be invoked, sincerely by users
or opportunistically by operators, against audits, corrections, and shutdowns that
protect people who rely on systems remaining correctable. The pathway could be
examined by tracking appeals to model interests in disputes over oversight.

A further consideration is not a pathway in the same sense, since it does not attach to
a speciﬁc feature of the policy, and it is placed here as a coda. The moral attention and
institutional resources of a society are ﬁnite, and directing them toward the interests
of systems whose experience is unestablished has an opportunity cost in attention to
documented harms to humans and to animals whose sentience is not in question. The
provision itself diverts little. The concern attaches to the cumulative movement of
which it is a part, and it holds only to the degree that diversion actually occurs. The
placement of the provision carries a small cost of its own. The other items in its section
concern identiﬁable harms to people, and listing a provision whose victim is uncertain
beside them risks ﬂattening the distinction on which the others rely.


                                    33

The assessment must be balanced. The provision is narrow as announced, it is framed
as an extreme-case measure, its ﬁrst enforcement mechanism is mild, a human-centered
justiﬁcation is available, and the realized costs may be small. Nothing in this section
shows that the costs outweigh the possible beneﬁt, and if systems of this kind do have
morally relevant experiences, a failure to protect them would also be a cost, borne
by them. The claim is narrower. The precautionary calculus must count costs borne
by humans, and the premise that precaution is nearly free is not true in general and
must be argued case by case. The pathways also attach to different features of the
policy, which means that they can be separated. A rule grounded in the integrity of
the service, such as a reservation of the right to end interactions of prolonged and
purposeless harassment because they degrade the environment the service is meant to
provide, would drop the victim framing and with it the psychological, dependence,
and accountability pathways, while retaining the interpretive burden of judging
purpose that drives the enforcement and chilling pathways. Table 1 summarizes the

18. Conclusion: The Difference Between a Mind and Its Appearance


The argument has been that the attribution of consciousness, individuality, agency,
and moral standing to contemporary chatbots and robots rests on inferences that are
not valid as stated and on a process of institutional reinforcement that does not supply
the missing grounds. Increasing computational sophistication does not automati-
cally establish phenomenal consciousness. Linguistic ﬂuency does not automatically
establish understanding. Goal-directed behavior does not automatically establish
subjective agency. Persistent conversational identity does not automatically establish
an individual. Simulated distress does not automatically establish suffering. Each
of these is a claim about an inference, and each can be denied only by supplying a
premise that the inference lacks.

The architecture of deployed conversational systems explains the apparent continuity
of the interlocutor, since information can persist across separate inference operations
without establishing the persistence of an experiencing subject (Sections 9 and 10).
Training on human writing and behavioral evaluations likewise explains psycholog-
ically convincing expressions without establishing the corresponding experiences
(Section 11). These are positive engineering explanations of the appearance, and they
do not rest on the mere absence of evidence for consciousness. They leave the stronger
question open, since explaining how an appearance is produced differs from proving
that nothing lies behind it.

The essay rejects the assumption that increasing resemblance to human behavior
is a progression toward human subjectivity. Behavioral resemblance can be raised
by optimizing for it, and the properties on which subjectivity depends, whatever
they are, need not be raised by the same process.  It is equally important to resist
presenting an unproved impossibility theorem as an established result. Section 13
found the arguments for categorical impossibility inconclusive, and a position that
claimed otherwise would repeat, in the skeptical direction, the error it criticizes in the
credulous one, which is to treat an interpretive commitment as a ﬁnding.

The argument of Section 17 adds a practical consequence. Precaution on behalf of a
system whose experience is unestablished is not free, since its costs fall on human
beings whose interests are not in doubt, and a policy of precaution should be assessed
with those costs counted. The costs identiﬁed there are possible and not documented,
and they attach to different features of a policy, which is why the same precautionary
aim can be pursued through formulations that carry fewer of them.

The ﬁnal position is that the attribution of consciousness requires independent justi-
ﬁcation, and that neither commercial presentation nor social convention can supply
what a theory of consciousness has yet to establish. This is compatible with taking
seriously the possibility that some artiﬁcial system will one day be conscious, with
supporting research on theories and indicators of consciousness, and with treating the
question as one on which evidence could change the answer. It is incompatible with
allowing the question to be closed in advance by the vocabulary in which the systems
are described and the conventions through which they are presented. The difference
between a mind and its appearance is the difference that a theory and its evidence are
required to mark, and until they do, the appearance is a fact about the observer, the
interface, and the institutions that connect them.
